core.text: To report that something *will* happen, Latin uses **the future infinitive (the 'going to' form: venturum esse)**: the future participle plus *esse*. He says *sē epistulam scrīptūrum esse* — that he will write a letter. The participle agrees with the accusative subject of the reported clause, so *sē … scrīptūram esse* for a woman, *eōs … factūrōs esse* for several men. Latin name: *īnfīnītīvus futūrī*.
*She hopes that he will come*: English keeps a future verb inside the *that*-clause. Latin puts the future on the infinitive instead.
Future participle (accusative, agreeing) + esse. Esse is often left out: dīcit sē ventūrum. Sum has futūrum esse or the one-word fore.

invented.la: Mārcus prōmittit sē bonum puerum futūrum esse.
invented.en: Marcus promises that he will be a good boy.

core.text: Three infinitives, three times. *Scrībere* — is writing (same time); **the perfect infinitive (the 'to have done' form)** *scrīpsisse* — wrote (earlier); *scrīptūrum esse* — will write (later). The -ūr- marks the future, the -isse the past.

more.text: The learner's notes (week 23) point out that English has nothing like this and translates with a *that*-clause and *will* or *would*: *audīvistis nōs profectūrōs esse* — you heard that we were going to leave. *Fore* is the short form of *futūrum esse*: after *spērō* — I hope — *eum brevī sānum fore*, that he will soon be well.

The future passive infinitive is supine + *īrī* (*laudātum īrī* — to be going to be praised); it never changes its ending and is rare. Ørberg shows it in cap. XXIII, where Aemilia fears her son *ā patre verberātum īrī*.

teach.title: Reporting what will happen

notice.ask: Tap the words that report what Julius and Julia will do — what do the two pairs have in common?

teach.say: When Latin reports that something *will* happen, the verb in the report becomes **the future infinitive (the 'going to' form: ventūrum esse)**. *Mārcus dīcit sē longam epistulam scrīptūrum esse* — Marcus says that he will write a long letter. English needs a 'that' and a 'will'; Latin packs both into the form.

teach.title: What the two words are
teach.say: It is the future participle (the 'about to' word: ventūrus = about to come) with *esse* after it: *scrīptūrum esse*, *datūrum esse*. The table prints its naming form, *scrīptūrus esse*, on the future row of the infinitives; inside a report the participle changes to *scrīptūrum* to agree with the accusative person.

show.say: scrīptūrus esse — the fourth part scrīpt- with -ūrus, then esse

teach.title: The participle agrees with the person reported
teach.say: The person reported stands in the accusative (the object form) — *sē*, *Iūlium*, *lupum* — and the participle agrees with it: *sē itūrum esse* for a man, *sē ventūram esse* for a woman, *sē lūsūrōs esse* for several. Only *esse* never changes.

teach.title: Telling it from the perfect infinitive
teach.say: Three infinitives, three times: *cantāre* — singing now; *cantāvisse* — sang, earlier; *cantātūram esse* — will sing, later. The *-isse* is the earlier one, the *-ūrum esse* the later one, and a sentence can carry both at once.

teach.title: The two short forms
teach.say: *Esse* is very often simply left out and understood: *Mārcus dīcit sē statim ventūrum*. And *sum* has a one-word future infinitive of its own, *fore*, beside the fuller *futūrum esse*: *Medicus dīcit puerum sānum fore* — the doctor says the boy will be well.
